title: Signals on the wire
subtitle: Signals, papers, essays, and field notes — selected for substance.
note: Prototype issue · public feeds only · the archive starts here.

items.title: Karpathy’s Pelican
items.dek: A live Hacker News item pointing to a public post, with the discussion kept beside the original source.
items.summary: The item is a useful test of the brief’s source boundary: a short public post is one object, the Hacker News thread is another, and neither should be padded into a larger claim than the links support.
items.deskNote: A compact signal, with the conversation left visible rather than collapsed into a verdict.

items.title: An autoregressive language model on a 6502 processor
items.dek: A small computing experiment that puts a language-model idea against an unusually constrained machine.
items.summary: The source is a technical build log about running an autoregressive language model on a 6502 processor. It belongs in the brief because the constraint is the subject: the story is about the shape of a system when the usual abundance of memory and compute disappears.
items.deskNote: A good counterweight to stories that assume scale before explaining the mechanism.

items.title: Shitty: a fast terminal with the trade-off left in the name
items.dek: A public repository that makes speed and memory safety an explicit tension instead of hiding it behind product language.
items.summary: This is a small repository-shaped story: a terminal project presents its performance claim alongside the cost it accepts. The useful part is not the name or the provocation, but the clarity of the trade-off exposed by the project’s own framing.
items.deskNote: The brief should make room for projects whose interesting idea is the trade-off, not the polish.

items.title: AskChem: claim-centred infrastructure for chemistry literature synthesis
items.dek: A paper proposing a literature-synthesis system organised around claims rather than ranked document lists.
items.summary: AskChem frames chemistry literature synthesis as a claim-finding problem: the relevant evidence is scattered across publications, so a useful system must help locate and assemble specific findings rather than stop at a ranked list of papers.
items.deskNote: The claim is the unit worth following; the document list is only the start of the work.

items.title: AISPA: auditing system prompts from the user side
items.dek: A paper about auditing system prompts in language-model applications, a layer that is often hidden from public view.
items.summary: AISPA treats system prompts as an object for audit. The paper’s premise is that these instructions govern application behaviour while remaining largely undisclosed, leaving a gap between the visible interface and the rules shaping the model underneath.
items.deskNote: A useful reminder that an AI product has an instruction layer before it has a user experience.

items.title: ReToken: one token for visual retrieval
items.dek: A paper addressing distractor-heavy visual context and the cost of processing every token at once.
items.summary: ReToken focuses on a familiar scaling problem in vision-language systems: long visual context becomes harder as distractors accumulate, while processing the whole context creates GPU-memory pressure. The proposed direction is to change the token representation rather than simply add more context.
items.deskNote: The interesting move is representational: less context may require better tokens, not only larger windows.

items.title: The Quieter Route
items.dek: A reading packet for travel that follows food, walking, ordinary life, and attention rather than a checklist.
items.summary: The first Lifestyle special gathers essays, newsletters, documentaries, podcasts, and ambient walks around a slower way of looking at place. It is a route into food culture, daily routines, local voices, and the small geography between famous sights.
items.deskNote: A field notebook for the kind of travel that leaves room for a second morning.
